catalog_quote: Polysyllables are generally stressed on the penult, with secondary stress on the pre-antepenult if any. However, there are two exceptions to this pattern. Where a monosyllable is reduplicated, stress falls on the final syllable: /zo'zo/ 'walk' cf. /zo/ 'go' /mi'mi/ 'see' The other exception involves certain words of three or more syllables in which stress falls on the antepenult (rather than the penult). For example: /'okene/ 'moon' /'kokolo/ 'round' /'ləgoto/ 'root' /'utini/ 'know' /'peputu/ 'tail' /mə'ləkana/ 'sky' /'koete/ 'fish' /bə'lukuru/ 'wing' /'mesiri/ 'red' /ta'dʒaluku/ 'scratch' It is noteworthy that in all words of this class, the vowels of the two last syllables are identical. It could therefore be argued that the final vowel is a surface echo vowel, and that these words are underlyingly consonant-final and do reflect the general pattern of penultimate stress. That is, we would reinterpret the trisyllables as disyllables (/'oken/, /'ləgot/, /'peput/ etc.) and the tetrasyllables as trisyllables (/mə'ləkan/, /bə'lukur/, /ta'dʒaluk/). (This would reflect their history; Ross 1988: 218.) Note that this pattern does not apply to all tri- and tetrasyllables which have identical vowels in the two last syllables. The words below have penultimate stress and must be interpreted as having an underlying final vowel: /ro'roko/ 'bird' /lu'lumu/ 'cold' /vovo'sele/ 'blow (of wind)'

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of polysyllabic words. Reduplicated monosyllables (CV-CV) take final stress. A lexical class of tri-/tetrasyllables whose last two vowels are identical takes antepenultimate stress; Ross analyses these as underlyingly consonant-final with a surface echo vowel, so that they too are penult-stressed underlyingly (but other words with identical final vowels, e.g. /ro'roko/ 'bird', /lu'lumu/ 'cold', have regular penult stress and an underlying final vowel).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on the pre-antepenult, if any (i.e. alternating leftward from the penult).
new_statements.exceptions: (1) reduplicated monosyllables: final stress (/zo'zo/ 'walk', /mi'mi/ 'see'); (2) echo-vowel class with antepenult stress (/'okene/ 'moon', /'ləgoto/ 'root', /'peputu/ 'tail', /'koete/ 'fish', /'mesiri/ 'red', /'kokolo/ 'round', /'utini/ 'know', /mə'ləkana/ 'sky', /bə'lukuru/ 'wing', /ta'dʒaluku/ 'scratch'), contrasted with penult-stressed /ro'roko/ 'bird', /lu'lumu/ 'cold', /vovo'sele/ 'blow (of wind)' (p.458). Also word-final /mu/ usually loses /u/ (/ramu/ -> [ram]).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress on citation forms from Ross's fieldnotes (speaker Moses Biliki, Ghaghara village); vowel length not phonemic; no discussion of phrase-level prosody or of stress under suffixation.
new_statements.identity_note: Ross 2002 describes Sisiqa proper ([si'siᵑga]; ethnonym Seqa/Sengga), central Choiseul, from speaker Moses Biliki of Ghaghara village = Glottolog sisi1250 exactly. Tryon & Hackman 1983 treat it as a dialect of 'East Choiseul' alongside Babatana (baba1268); Ross treats it as a separate language. No ISO code.

sources.note: Sec. 1.2 'Phonotactics and stress', p.457: polysyllables generally stressed on the penult, secondary stress on the pre-antepenult; exceptions: reduplicated monosyllables are final-stressed (/zo'zo/ 'walk', /mi'mi/ 'see'); a class of 3+-syllable words with identical last two vowels has antepenult stress (/'okene/ 'moon', /mə'ləkana/ 'sky'), which Ross suggests are underlyingly consonant-final with a surface echo vowel (so regular penult); but /ro'roko/ 'bird', /lu'lumu/ 'cold', /vovo'sele/ have penult stress (p.458). Vowel length not phonemic (p.456). No other stress mentions pp.459-466.
